title: Pick the best of ten, no going back
hook: Ten candidates, one look each. Is picking the best hopeless, or can a rule help?

doesNotKnow: that there is a best 'look then leap' rule

misconception: Choosing the best of ten candidates one at a time with no going back is hopeless, about 10%, or any early pick is as good as another.
objective: The learner can explain that rejecting the first few candidates and then taking the first one better than all before gives about a 40% chance of the very best out of ten, far above 10%.
keyState: The learner has played 20 rounds with Reject 3 (7 wins in batch 0) and with Reject 0 (1 win), on the same candidates.

claims.text: Model: 10 candidates arrive in random order, each is ranked only against those already seen, a refusal is final, and the rule is 'reject the first k, then take the first candidate better than everyone before; if none, end with the last'. Stated on the stage.
claims.source: Secretary problem set-up (Ferguson 1989, Statistical Science 4(3): 282-289). Stage text 'Toy: 10 candidates in random order, no going back.' | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Demo.tsx order()/pickIndex() implement exactly this rule; stage label states it. Set-up as in Ferguson (1989), 'Who solved the secretary problem?', Statistical Science 4(3): 282-289.

claims.text: Rejecting the first 3 of 10 and then taking the first one better than all before wins the best candidate 39.9% of the time (0.3987); rejecting none (taking the first) wins 10%.
claims.source: Exact: (k/n) sum_{j=k+1..n} 1/(j-1); node enumeration of all 10! = 3,628,800 orders: k=0 0.1000, 1 0.2829, 2 0.3658, 3 0.3987, 4 0.3983, 5 0.3728 (formula and enumeration agree). The question's options use exact(3) and 1/N from the same function. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node, my own enumeration of all 3,628,800 orders (Heap's algorithm): k=0..5 = 0.10000, 0.28290, 0.36579, 0.39869, 0.39825, 0.37282.

claims.text: Rejecting 4 does about as well as rejecting 3: 39.8%.
claims.source: Same enumeration, k = 4: 0.39825. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Same enumeration: k=4 0.39825, pct1 = 39.8%.

claims.text: In the first 20 rounds shown, Reject 3 won 7 and Reject 0 won 1 (the same 20 shuffled lists for both). This is one small run; the seeds are the first tried and were not tuned.
claims.source: mulberry32(b * 1000 + r + 1), batch b = 0, rounds r = 0..19 (batchWins(0,3) = 7, batchWins(0,0) = 1; node). Other batches in node: reject 3 wins 10, 10, 5; reject 0 wins 3, 3, 4. Seeds untuned. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node: batch 0 reject-3 wins 7, reject-0 wins 1; batches 1-3: 10/3, 10/3, 5/4.

claims.text: For long lists the best start is about 37% of the way through, and the chance of the very best is then about 37%.
claims.source: Limit n/e (about 0.368) as n grows (Ferguson 1989, Statistical Science 4(3): 282-289; verify the page range). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node n = 1000: optimal k = 368, win 0.3682; limit 1/e = 0.3679 (Ferguson 1989).

recall.question: You must pick the best of 10 candidates seen one by one, with no going back. What is a good rule?
options: Take the first one: any pick is as good as another
Reject the first few, then take the first one better than all of them
Wait until the very last one
recall.why: The rejected few set a yardstick. Rejecting about 3 or 4 of 10 wins the best about 40% of the time, against 10% for picking blindly.
